Of course I've also learned it all depends on what potatoes you use for mashing. Yukon golds are terrible for mashing, too firm, they take forever to get soft enough to be worth the effort, but they're great for making french fries. Gotta keep them slender though: Julienne or Medallion cuts for best results. Idaho browns are great for mashing and baking, they go soft quick.

Oddly enough, the red russets seem to be the perfect potato, depending on how you cut them. Dice them up small and they fry and mash quickly and beautifully. Quarter them for steaming or slow cooking and they hold their shape well. Keep them whole for baking and they develop a lovely, velvety texture that just can't be beat.

That said, for soups, stews, and sauces, this actually does work pretty well without damaging the dish or increasing the end result. For best results, scrub an Idaho brown clean, halve it, drop it in, and stir it up. After about ten minutes or so, fish out the potato halves and discard. You can bundle them in a fabric known as cheesecloth and tie it off with a clean twist tie or paper clip. This works best with dishes that have a high water content, because the salt moves more easily from the liquid into the potato.
